Markdown
# Outline

Outline is a source code summarizer utility designed to provide a quick, high-level overview of your codebase. It generates a summary of your code as an outline by prioritizing file paths and selected lines of code (LOC) based on a scoring scheme. It's a useful tool for developers who want a quick overview of a large codebase, or to keep track of the main points of their own projects.

## How it works

Outline performs a breadth-first traversal over your codebase, starting from the provided root nodes. By default, the root node is the current directory.

The utility produces a summary with a maximum number of lines specified by the user. The default maximum is 10 lines.

The scoring scheme of Outline prioritizes file paths over LOC. Within LOC, lines that contain certain keywords (e.g., `class`) are scored higher. This behavior can be modified as needed.

## Usage

You can use Outline from the command line as follows:

```bash
$ python main.py -r <root_node_1> <root_node_2> ... -l <max_lines>

Bash
$ python main.py -r ./main ./utils -l 20

Bash
$ python main.py

Bash
$ python -m unittest discover -s test
This README provides a general overview of Outline, how it works, how to use it, and some other standard sections for open source projects.

Ah, this is because the temporary script generated tries to import a module that isn't locally cached or present in a go.mod file.

The new Go module system expects dependencies to be managed via a go.mod file, especially if you're outside the GOPATH. But we're dynamically creating Go files, so we don't have a go.mod.

There are multiple solutions to this:

Run Outside of GOPATH with a Temporary go.mod:

We can create a temporary directory.

Then run go mod init tmp inside.

Copy the script to this directory and run it.

Run Within GOPATH:

If you run the script inside a directory which is under GOPATH, and the package github.com/bitfield/script is already downloaded, you won't face this issue. But this isn't a universal solution since newer Go practices suggest working outside of GOPATH using modules.

Use GOPATH Mode:

We can use environment variable GO111MODULE=off to turn off the module system temporarily and revert to GOPATH mode, but this requires that the dependencies be already installed in the GOPATH.

En Visual Studio Code, puedes configurar la función de guardado automático mediante la modificación de las preferencias del editor. Aquí tienes los pasos para habilitar el guardado automático:

Abre Visual Studio Code.

Ve a "File" (Archivo) en la esquina superior izquierda.

Selecciona "Preferences" (Preferencias), y luego selecciona "Settings" (Configuración).

Esto abrirá una nueva pestaña con las configuraciones. En la esquina superior derecha, verás un icono de engranaje; haz clic en él y selecciona "Settings".

Ahora, puedes buscar "Auto Save" en la barra de búsqueda.

Busca la opción llamada "Auto Save" y configúrala según tus preferencias. Puedes elegir entre diferentes modos, como "afterDelay" (después de un retraso), "onFocusChange" (al cambiar de foco) o "onWindowChange" (al cambiar de ventana).

Además, puedes configurar "Auto Save Delay" para establecer el tiempo de espera (en milisegundos) si seleccionaste "afterDelay".

Una vez que hayas configurado estas opciones, Visual Studio Code guardará automáticamente tus cambios según la configuración que hayas seleccionado.

Ten en cuenta que estas instrucciones se aplican a Visual Studio Code, que es un editor de código ligero. Si te refieres a Visual Studio (la versión completa de Microsoft), el proceso podría ser ligeramente diferente. import anvil.server
from pymongo import MongoClient
import unittest

# Connect to MongoDB
client = MongoClient("mongodb://localhost:27017/")
db = client["line_db"]
collection = db["line_data"]

@anvil.server.callable
def store_line_data(people, time_taken):
    data = {"people": people, "time_taken": time_taken}
    collection.insert_one(data)
    return "Data stored successfully."

@anvil.server.callable
def estimate_line_time(current_people):
    all_data = list(collection.find({}))
    total_people = 0
    total_time = 0
    
    for data in all_data:
        total_people += data["people"]
        total_time += data["time_taken"]
        
    if total_people == 0:
        return "Insufficient data."
    
    avg_time_per_person = total_time / total_people
    estimated_time = avg_time_per_person * current_people
    
    return f"Estimated time: {estimated_time} minutes"

# Unit Test
class TestLineFunctions(unittest.TestCase):
    
    def test_store_line_data(self):
        result = store_line_data(10, 20)
        self.assertEqual(result, "Data stored successfully.")
        
    def test_estimate_line_time(self):
        store_line_data(10, 20)
        store_line_data(20, 40)
        result = estimate_line_time(15)
        self.assertEqual(result, "Estimated time: 30.0 minutes")

    anvil.server.connect("YOUR_ANVIL_UPLINK_KEY")

In the context of Anvil, data_tables and app_tables serve different purposes:

data_tables: This term is used in the anvil.yaml file to define the schema of the Data Tables within your Anvil app. It's a way to specify what tables and columns your app should have if you're defining your app through code and version control.

app_tables: This is a Python module you import in your Anvil server code to interact with the Data Tables. It provides methods to query, add, update, and delete rows in your tables. You use app_tables in your server functions to perform database operations.

Since you're not using Anvil Uplink and are defining everything within the Anvil environment, you can absolutely use app_tables in your server code to interact with the Data Tables you've defined.

So, in summary:

Use data_tables in your anvil.yaml to define the schema.

Use app_tables in your server code to interact with those tables.

import networkx as nx
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def analyze_graph(G: nx.Graph):
    """
    Analyzes various properties of the given graph, including its diameter, clustering coefficient,
    and degree distribution.

    :param G: A NetworkX graph object.
    """
    # Check if the graph is connected; this is required to compute the diameter
    if nx.is_connected(G):
        diameter = nx.diameter(G)
        print(f"Diameter of the graph: {diameter}")
    else:
        print("Graph is not connected; diameter of the giant component will be calculated.")
        # Find the largest connected component (giant component)
        giant_component = max(nx.connected_components(G), key=len)
        G_giant = G.subgraph(giant_component).copy()

        # Compute the diameter of the giant component
        diameter = nx.diameter(G_giant)
        print(f"Diameter of the giant component: {diameter}")

    # Compute the average clustering coefficient of the graph
    avg_clustering = nx.average_clustering(G)
    print(f"Average Clustering Coefficient: {avg_clustering}")

    # Calculate and plot the degree distribution of the graph
    degrees = [G.degree(n) for n in G.nodes()]
    degree_counts = np.bincount(degrees)
    plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
    plt.bar(range(len(degree_counts)), degree_counts, width=0.80, color='b')
    plt.title("Degree Distribution")
    plt.xlabel("Degree")
    plt.ylabel("Frequency")
    plt.show()

                torch.zeros(batch_size, self.hidden_dim, height, width, device=device))

class ConvLSTM(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, hidden_dim, kernel_size, num_layers, batch_first=True, bias=True, return_all_layers=False):
        super(ConvLSTM, self).__init__()
        self.input_dim = input_dim
        self.hidden_dim = hidden_dim
        self.kernel_size = kernel_size
        self.num_layers = num_layers
        self.batch_first = batch_first
        self.bias = bias
        self.return_all_layers = return_all_layers

        cell_list = []
        for i in range(self.num_layers):
            cur_input_dim = self.input_dim if i == 0 else self.hidden_dim[i - 1]
            cell_list.append(ConvLSTMCell(input_dim=cur_input_dim,
                                          hidden_dim=self.hidden_dim[i],
                                          kernel_size=self.kernel_size,
                                          bias=self.bias))
        self.cell_list = nn.ModuleList(cell_list)

    def forward(self, input_tensor, hidden_state=None):
        # Assuming input_tensor is of shape (batch, seq_len, channels, height, width)
        if not self.batch_first:
            # Convert to (batch, seq_len, channels, height, width)
            input_tensor = input_tensor.permute(1, 0, 2, 3, 4)

        b, _, _, h, w = input_tensor.size()

        if hidden_state is None:
            # Initialize hidden state if not provided
            hidden_state = [self.cell_list[i].init_hidden(b, (h, w)) for i in range(self.num_layers)]

        current_input = input_tensor
        layer_output_list = []
        last_state_list = []

        for layer_idx in range(self.num_layers):
            h, c = hidden_state[layer_idx]
            output_inner = []
            for t in range(current_input.size(1)):
                h, c = self.cell_list[layer_idx](current_input[:, t, :, :, :], (h, c))
                output_inner.append(h)

            layer_output = torch.stack(output_inner, dim=1)
            current_input = layer_output

            layer_output_list.append(layer_output)
            last_state_list.append((h, c))

        if not self.return_all_layers:
            layer_output_list = layer_output_list[-1:]
            last_state_list = last_state_list[-1:]

        return layer_output_list, last_state_list

class ImageSequencePredictor(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, input_dim, hidden_dim, kernel_size, num_layers, output_size=(128, 128)):
        super(ImageSequencePredictor, self).__init__()
        self.output_size = output_size

        # Simple CNN
        self.conv_layers = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(1, 64, kernel_size=7, stride=2, padding=3, bias=False),
            nn.BatchNorm2d(64),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),
        )

        # ConvLSTM layer
        self.conv_lstm = ConvLSTM(
            input_dim=64,  # Simple CNN output
            hidden_dim=hidden_dim,  # Hidden dims
            kernel_size=kernel_size,  # kernel size
            num_layers=num_layers,  # layers nmber
            batch_first=True,
            bias=True,
            return_all_layers=False
        )

        # transpose conv to generate images
        self.trans_conv = nn.Sequential(
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(hidden_dim[-1], 64, kernel_size=3, stride=2),
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, 32, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),  # sencod layer
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(32, 16, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),  # third layer
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(16, 8, kernel_size=3, stride=2, padding=1),  # Forth layer
            nn.ReLU(),
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(8, 1, kernel_size=2, stride=2),  # final output
            nn.Sigmoid()
            )

    def forward(self, x):
        batch_size, timesteps, C, H, W = x.size()
        x = x.view(batch_size * timesteps, C, H, W)
        x = self.conv_layers(x)

        # Rsize dims
        x = x.view(batch_size, timesteps, -1, H // 4, W // 4)
        layer_output_list, last_state_list = self.conv_lstm(x)

        # Use the final CNN time
        x = last_state_list[-1][0]  # The final states

        # Change the size
        x = self.trans_conv(x)

        # resize the output
        x = F.interpolate(x, size=self.output_size, mode='bilinear', align_corners=False)

        return x

rounds.Answer:
The Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) is a metric used to evaluate the quality of a reconstructed or compressed image. It measures the ratio between the maximum possible power of a signal (in this case, the original image) and the power of corrupting noise (differences between the original and reconstructed images).

The PSNR is often expressed in decibels (dB) and is calculated using the formula:

PSNR=10⋅log⁡10(MAX2MSE)\text{PSNR} = 10 \cdot \log_{10} \left( \frac{{\text{MAX}^2}}{{\text{MSE}}} \right)PSNR=10⋅log10​(MSEMAX2​)

where:

    def __init__(self, in_channels, out_channels):

        # Encoder

        self.encoder_pool = nn.MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2)

        # Decoder

        x = torch.cat([x, encoder_output], dim=1)  # Concatenate with encoder output
        x = self.decoder_conv(x)

        return x

The choice between cookies and local storage for storing data depends on various factors and the specific requirements of your application. Here are some considerations to help you decide:

Cookies:

Compatibility: Cookies are widely supported across different browsers.

Storage Limit: Cookies have a smaller storage limit (typically around 4KB) compared to local storage.

Automatic Sending: Cookies are automatically sent with every HTTP request, which can add overhead to network traffic.

Expiration: Cookies can be set with an expiration date, allowing them to persist for a specific duration.

Server-Side Access: Cookies can be accessed and manipulated on the server-side, which can be useful for certain server interactions.

Local Storage:

Storage Limit: Local storage offers a larger storage capacity (typically around 5MB) compared to cookies.

Simplicity: Local storage provides a simpler and more straightforward API for storing and retrieving data.

Data Retention: Data stored in local storage remains intact even after the browser is closed and reopened.

Client-Side Access: Local storage is accessible and manipulable only on the client-side, making it more suitable for client-centric applications.

No Automatic Sending: Local storage data is not automatically sent with each HTTP request, reducing network traffic.

Based on these factors, local storage is generally preferred for storing larger amounts of data on the client-side, while cookies are often used for smaller amounts of data and scenarios where server-side access is required.

It's important to note that both cookies and local storage have their own security considerations, and you should be mindful of storing sensitive information in either of them.

Ultimately, the choice between cookies and local storage depends on your specific use case, the amount of data you need to store, the compatibility requirements, and the desired behavior of your application.

title : - Mobility Management for Hybrid LiFi and WiFi
Networks in the Presence of Light-path Blockage

Abstract—Hybrid light fidelity (LiFi) and wireless fidelity
(WiFi) networks (HLWNets) have been recently proposed as a
promising technique for indoor wireless communications. Such
a network combines the high-speed transmission of LiFi and
the ubiquitous coverage of WiFi. Meanwhile, in addition to user
mobility, intermittent light-path blockages make the handover
issue intricate in HLWNets. Also, load balancing (LB) is necessary
because the coverage areas of LiFi and WiFi networks are
completely overlapped. This further increases the difficulty in
handover as the decision for a vertical or a horizontal handover
in a mobile environment with ultra-small cells is non-trival.
Aimed at providing an optimal solution to the access point
selection (APS) with given channel state information (CSI), the
conventional LB method might cause frequent and unnecessary
handovers. In this paper, a joint optimisation problem is formulated to simultaneously consider LB and handover in HLWNets.
Results show that compared with the conventional LB method,
the proposed method can improve the system throughput by up
to 60%.
Index Terms—Light fidelity (LiFi), hybrid network, handover,
user mobility, light-path blockage

introduction :-
GLOBAL mobile data traffic is expected to grow over 4
times in 4 years, reaching 48.3 exabytes per month at
the end of 2021 [1]. The exponentially increasing demand for
mobile data is about to outstrip the spectrum capacity of radiofrequency (RF) in the near future, leading to the looming crisis
of a spectrum crunch [2]. In order to exploit the spectrum
of higher frequencies, visible light communication (VLC)
and its use for wireless networking, which is termed light
fidelity (LiFi) [3], have drawn significant research attention
in recent years. LiFi modulates the light intensity of lightemitting diodes (LEDs) to carry information bits and employs
photodiodes (PDs) to detect the transmitted signals. LiFi can
offer many advantages over wireless fidelity (WiFi), including
access to a much wider and unregulated spectrum, more secure
communications and the ability to be used in RF-restricted
areas. Moreover, LiFi is capable of providing high-speed data
transmissions in the range of Gbps [3].
A LiFi access point (AP) usually covers a relatively small
area, of approximately 2-3m in diameter. In order to combine
the high-speed transmission of LiFi and the ubiquitous coverage of WiFi, hybrid LiFi and WiFi networks (HLWNets)
are developed. Such a network is able to achieve a greater
throughput than a stand-alone LiFi or WiFi network [4].
Meanwhile, the issue of access point selection (APS) becomes
challenging mainly due to two reasons: i) WiFi APs have
relatively large coverage areas but limited system capacities in
comparison to LiFi APs; and ii) the coverage areas of different
networks overlap each other. Using the signal strength strategy
(SSS) method, which assigns a user to the AP offering the
highest received signal power, would render the WiFi system
susceptible to traffic overloads. Thus load balancing (LB) is
essential for HLWNets. Studies are carried out in this field
in [5]–[7], but they are all focused on optimising the instant
system throughput and might result in frequent handovers.
In a hybrid network there are two types of handovers:
horizontal handover (HHO) and vertical handover (VHO).
HHOs occur within the domain of a single wireless access
technology, whereas VHOs happen between different wireless
access technologies. Due to different medium access control
protocols, a VHO normally causes a much longer delay than
a HHO [8]. Therefore frequent VHOs would significantly
reduce the system capacity of a HLWNet. Only a few studies
consider the handover cost caused by user mobility in a LiFiinvolved hybrid network, e.g. [9]. Light-path blockages are
another significant factor that causes handovers in HLWNets
[10]. However, this research field is underdeveloped in the
current literature. When light-path blockages happen to a LiFi
user, it can be transferred to WiFi until the LiFi connectivity is restored. But if light-path blockages occur frequently,
conducting the above action could potentially result in an
overall throughput even lower. Thus it is vital to selectively
switch LiFi users to WiFi when they experience light-path
blockages. Taking both user mobility and light-path blockages
into account, the LB issue becomes more complicated. To
the best of the authors’ acknowledge, this issue has not been
addressed so far.
In this paper, a novel APS method is proposed for HLWNets
by jointly performing LB and handover. Specifically, the
handover cost caused by both user mobility and light-path
blockages is involved in the optimisation problem of LB.
Instead of choosing a specific AP at a given time instant,
the proposed method determines the type of network access
for each user over a period of time. Within this period, the
users can only be transferred among homogeneous APs as
long as the light path is not blocked. In the event of a lightpath blockage, selective LiFi users are allowed to temporarily access the WiFi network.
The remainder of this paper is organised as follows. In
Section II, the system model of an indoor HLWNet is described, including the network deployment and channel model.
A conventional LB method is introduced in Section III, and
a novel method is proposed in Section IV. Simulation results
are presented in Section V. Finally, conclusions are drawn in
Section VI.

II. SYSTEM MODEL
An indoor HLWNet consisting of one WiFi AP and a
number of LiFi APs is considered. The WiFi AP is deployed
on the ground and in the centre of the room, whereas each
LiFi AP is integrated into the ceiling LED lamps, which face
downward vertically. Note that the WiFi AP provides coverage
for the entire room, while each LiFi AP covers a confined area.
The LiFi APs operate with different spectra and thus do not
interfere with each other. The mobile users are assumed to
follow the random waypoint (RWP) model [11]. The user’s
speed is a random variable uniformly distributed between
0 and a maximum speed. During the period of interest the
user’s speed is assumed to be constant. Each user is equipped
with a upward-oriented PD and can only be connected to one
AP. Time-division multiple accessing (TDMA) is employed to
enable the APs to serve multiple users.

import numpy as np
from typing import List

class LifiAccessPoint:
    def __init__(self, x, y, Φ_1by2=60, Apd=100*1e-4, ref_index=1.5, FOV=90, gf=1,
            room_x=5, room_y=5, room_z=5, h=0.8, Rpd=0.53, pw=0.8, Popt=3, k=3, Nlifi=1e-21, Blifi=20*1e6):
        # attribute for Half-intensity radiation angle (Φ1/2)
        self.Φ_1by2 = Φ_1by2 * np.pi / 180
        self.m = -np.log(2) / np.log(np.cos(np.radians(Φ_1by2)))
        # Refractive ref_index of the medium
        self.ref_index = ref_index
        # FoV semi-angle of PD, Ψmax
        self.FOV = FOV * np.pi / 180
        # physical area of the PD, Apd
        self.Apd = Apd
        # gain of the optical filter, gf
        self.gf = gf
        # length of the room in the x-direction (horizontal) in meters.
        self.room_x = room_x
        # length of the room in the y-direction (vertical) in meters.
        self.room_y = room_y
        # height of the room in meters
        self.room_z = room_z
        # height of the user above the receiver plane
        self.h = h
        # position of the lifi access point in ceiling
        self.lifi_position = np.array([x, y, room_z])
        # Detector responsivity, Rpd
        self.Rpd = Rpd
        # Transmitted optical power per LiFi AP, Popt
        self.Popt = Popt
        # optical to electrical conversion coefficient, k
        self.k = k
        # PSD of noise in LiFi AP, NLiFi
        self.Nlifi = Nlifi
        # Bandwidth of LiFi AP, BLiFi
        self.Blifi = Blifi
        # Wall reflectivity, pw
        self.pw = pw

        # Number of points in the x and y directions
        self.Nx = int(room_x * 10)
        self.Ny = int(room_y * 10)
        self.x = np.linspace(0, room_x, self.Nx)
        self.y = np.linspace(0, room_y, self.Ny)
        self.XR, self.YR = np.meshgrid(self.x, self.y)

    def get_channel_gain(self, user_x, user_y):
        # uncomment this line to include NLOS channel gain
        return self.channel_gain_los(user_x, user_y) #+ self.channel_gain_nlos(user_x, user_y)

    def channel_gain_los(self, user_x, user_y):
        d = self.distance(user_x, user_y)
        # both angles are equal due to symmetry
        incidence = self.angle_incidence(user_x, user_y)
        irradiance = incidence
        gc = self.optical_gain(incidence)
        channel_gain = ((self.m + 1) * self.Apd * (np.cos(irradiance)**self.m) * np.cos(incidence) * self.gf * gc) / (2 * np.pi * (d**2))
        # print(incidence, irradiance, channel_gain, self.m, gc, self.Apd, self.gf)
        return channel_gain

    def channel_gain_nlos(self, user_x, user_y):
        boxes_per_meter = 10
        dl, dh = 1/boxes_per_meter, 1/boxes_per_meter
        height_coord = np.arange(self.h, self.room_z, dh)
        length_coord = np.arange(self.h, self.room_x, dl)
        user_position = np.array([user_x, user_y, self.h])
        integration = 0

        for height in height_coord:
            print(f'{height:.3f}  ')
            for length in length_coord:
                locations = [np.array([length, 0, height]), np.array([length, self.room_y, height]),
                            np.array([0, length, height]), np.array([self.room_x, length, height])]
                for curr_location in locations:
                    d_iw = np.linalg.norm(curr_location - self.lifi_position)
                    d_wu = np.linalg.norm(user_position - curr_location)
                    theta_iw = np.arccos((self.room_z - height) / d_iw)
                    ϑ_iw = 90 - theta_iw
                    phi_wu = np.arccos((height - self.h) / d_wu)
                    ϑ_wu = 90 - phi_wu
                    numerator = (self.m + 1) * self.Apd * self.pw * (np.cos(theta_iw)**self.m) * \
                                self.gf * self.optical_gain(phi_wu) * np.cos(phi_wu) * np.cos(ϑ_iw) * np.cos(ϑ_wu)
                    integration += (numerator * dl * dh) / (2 * (np.pi * d_iw * d_wu)**2)
        return integration

    def signal_to_noise_ratio(self, user_x, user_y, otherLifiAPs:List):
        summation_term = 0
        for lifi in otherLifiAPs:
            # print(f'Lifi at {lifi.lifi_position} has gain', lifi.get_channel_gain(user_x, user_y))
            summation_term += (lifi.Rpd * lifi.get_channel_gain(user_x, user_y) * lifi.Popt / lifi.k) ** 2
        # print('self gain: ', self.get_channel_gain(user_x, user_y))
        numerator = (self.Rpd * self.get_channel_gain(user_x, user_y) * self.Popt / self.k) ** 2
        # uncomment this line to include noise from other LiFi APs
        denominator = self.Nlifi * self.Blifi + summation_term
        # print(f'numerator: {numerator}, denominator: {denominator}, sum: {summation_term}')
        return numerator / denominator

    def distance(self, user_x, user_y):
        user_position = np.array([user_x, user_y, self.h])
        distance =  np.linalg.norm(user_position - self.lifi_position)
        return distance

    def optical_gain(self, angle_incidence):
        if 0 <= angle_incidence <= self.FOV:
            return (self.ref_index**2) / (np.sin(self.FOV)**2)
        else:
            return 0

    def angle_incidence(self, user_x, user_y):
        d = self.distance(user_x, user_y)
        return np.arccos((self.room_z - self.h) / d)

class WiFiAccessPoint:
    def __init__(self, ap_id, ap_position, transmit_power, noise_psd, bandwidth,sigma):

        self.ap_position = ap_position
        self.transmit_power = transmit_power
        self.noise_psd = noise_psd
        self.bandwidth = bandwidth
        self.sigma = sigma

    def calculate_channel_gain_rayleigh(self,k):
        X0 = np.exp(1j * np.radians(45))
        X1 = np.random.normal(0, 1) + 1j * np.random.normal(0, 1)
        H = np.sqrt(k / (k + 1)) * X0 + np.sqrt(1 / (k + 1)) * X1
        return np.abs(H)

    def calculate_distance(self, user_position):

        return np.linalg.norm(np.array(user_position) - np.array(self.ap_position))

        distance = self.calculate_distance(user.position)
        dref = 5.0  # Breakdown distance, d_BP (in meters)

def fibonacci_memo(n, memo={}):
    # Check if the result is already calculated and stored in memo
    if n in memo:
        return memo[n]
    
    # Base case
    if n <= 1:
        return n
    
    # Recursive step
    result = fibonacci_memo(n - 1, memo) + fibonacci_memo(n - 2, memo)
    
    # Store the result in memo
    memo[n] = result
    
    return result

def fibonacci_tabulation(n):
    # Create an array to store Fibonacci numbers, initialized with zeros
    fib = [0] * (n + 1)
    
    # Base cases
    fib[0] = 0
    fib[1] = 1
    
    # Calculate Fibonacci numbers from the bottom up
    for i in range(2, n + 1):
        fib[i] = fib[i - 1] + fib[i - 2]
    
    return fib[n]

    coins.sort(reverse=True)  # Sort coins in descending order
    if amount == 0:
        return 0
    if amount < 0 or not coins:
        return float('inf')
    if (len(coins), amount) in memo:
        return memo[(len(coins), amount)]

    include_last_coin = 1 + make_change_min_coins(coins, amount - coins[0], memo)  # Use coins[0] as it is now the largest coin
    exclude_last_coin = make_change_min_coins(coins[1:], amount, memo)

    memo[(len(coins), amount)] = min(include_last_coin, exclude_last_coin)

    return memo[(len(coins), amount)]

# Example usage
coins = [25, 1, 10, 5]
amount = 73
min_coins = make_change_min_coins(coins, amount)
print(f"Minimum number of coins to make {amount} cents with coins: {min_coins}")

Absolutely, let's delve into the distinctions between memoization and tabulation in dynamic programming:

Memoization:

Top-Down Approach:

Involves solving the problem in a recursive manner, breaking it down into smaller subproblems.

The solutions to subproblems are stored in a data structure (often a dictionary or cache) to avoid redundant calculations.

It starts from the original problem and works its way down to the base cases.

Recursive Calls:

Recursive calls are made for subproblems, and solutions are retrieved from the memo (cache) if already calculated.

It's often more intuitive and easier to implement for certain problems, especially those that naturally exhibit overlapping subproblems.

Memory Usage:

Memory usage depends on the depth of the recursion and the number of unique subproblems.

Can potentially save memory by not calculating solutions for the same subproblem multiple times.

Tabulation:

Bottom-Up Approach:

Involves solving the problem iteratively, starting from the base cases and building up to the final solution.

It uses a table (usually a one-dimensional or multi-dimensional array) to store solutions to subproblems.

Iterative Filling:

The table is filled iteratively, often using nested loops to cover all subproblems in a specific order.

It starts from the base cases and progressively computes solutions for larger subproblems until reaching the final solution.

Memory Usage:

Memory usage depends on the size of the table, which is determined by the dimensions of the problem.

Can potentially use more memory than memoization for certain problems, especially those with sparse solutions.

Differences in Data Structures:

Memoization:

Typically involves using a cache (dictionary) to store solutions to subproblems.

The key in the cache is often a tuple representing the state of the problem (e.g., (i, j) for a two-dimensional problem).

Tabulation:

Involves using an array or multiple arrays to store solutions to subproblems.

The indices of the array correspond to different states of the problem (e.g., dp[i] for a one-dimensional problem or dp[i][j] for a two-dimensional problem).

Memory Efficiency Consideration:

Memoization:

Can potentially save memory by only calculating solutions for unique subproblems.

Well-suited for problems with a recursive structure that leads to overlapping subproblems.

Tabulation:

Fills out the entire table, even for subproblems with non-unique solutions.

Well-suited for problems where there is no significant memory advantage to skipping repeated calculations.

In summary, while both memoization and tabulation involve filling out a table, they differ in their approaches and the way they store and retrieve solutions to subproblems. Memoization involves a top-down recursive approach with a cache, while tabulation involves a bottom-up iterative approach with a table. The choice between them often depends on the specific characteristics of the problem at hand.

import requests

def get_total_reactions(owner, repo, issue_number, token):
    url = f"https://api.github.com/repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{issue_number}/reactions"
    headers = {
        'Authorization': f'token {token}',
        'Accept': 'application/vnd.github.squirrel-girl-preview+json'
    }
    response = requests.get(url, headers=headers)
    if response.status_code == 200:
        reactions = response.json()
        total_reactions = sum(reaction['count'] for reaction in reactions)
        return total_reactions
    else:
        print(f"Failed to retrieve reactions: {response.status_code}")
        return None

#!/bin/bash

# Fetch all issues with label 'RFC' from the repository 'leanprover/lean4'
issues=$(gh api repos/leanprover/lean4/issues --paginate --jq '.[] | select(.labels[].name == "RFC") | {url: .html_url, created_at: .created_at, updated_at: .updated_at, number: .number}')

# Parse each issue and print desired details
echo "$issues" | jq -r '. | @base64' | while read line; do
    _jq() {
        echo ${line} | base64 --decode | jq -r ${1}
    }
    url=$(_jq '.url')
    created_at=$(_jq '.created_at')
    updated_at=$(_jq '.updated_at')
    issue_number=$(_jq '.number')

    # Fetch the total number of reactions for each issue
    total_reactions=$(gh api repos/leanprover/lean4/issues/$issue_number/reactions --paginate --jq 'length')

    # Print the results
    echo "Issue URL: $url"
    echo "Created at: $created_at"
    echo "Last modified: $updated_at"
    echo "Total reactions: $total_reactions"
    echo ""
done

The graph above represents the 'Elbow Method'. This method is a heuristic used in determining the number of clusters in a data set. The idea is to run k-means clustering on the dataset for a range of values of k (say, k from 1 to 10), and for each value of k, calculate the sum of squared errors (SSE).

The idea is that we want a small SSE, but that the SSE tends to decrease toward 0 as we increase k (the SSE is 0 when k is equal to the number of data points in the dataset, because then each data point is its own cluster, and there is no error between it and the center of its cluster). The highest bit (the leftmost bit, also known as the sign bit) is used to determine the sign of the number. A 1 in this position indicates a negative number.

For the most negative number (1000 0000), flipping all the bits gives 0111 1111 (which is 127 in decimal), and adding 1 to this gives 1000 0000 again, confirming its value as -128 when reverted back to two's complement form.

Thus, -128 is indeed the lowest value that can be represented with an 8-bit two's complement encoded signal.

If your dataset is not labeled or scored, you'll need to create a labeled dataset for training your AI model. This process is known as manual annotation or labeling. Here's a general approach you can follow:

Define Evaluation Criteria:

Clearly define the criteria you want to use to grade the solutions. This could be based on the quality, feasibility, innovation, or any other relevant factors related to circular economy solutions.

Create an Annotation Guide:

Develop an annotation guide that provides clear instructions to human annotators on how to assign scores based on the defined criteria. This guide helps ensure consistency in the annotations.

Select Annotators:

Choose annotators who have a good understanding of the evaluation criteria and can provide reliable judgments. This could be domain experts, professionals in the field, or individuals trained specifically for this task.

Annotation Process:

Have annotators review each solution and assign scores based on the criteria. You can use a scale (e.g., 1 to 5) or any other scoring system that fits your evaluation criteria.

Quality Control:

Implement a quality control process to ensure the reliability of annotations. This may involve having multiple annotators independently evaluate a subset of the solutions, and then comparing their scores to identify and address discrepancies.

Build the Labeled Dataset:

Compile the annotated data into a labeled dataset. Each entry should include the text description of the solution and the assigned scores.

Data Splitting:

Split the labeled dataset into training and testing sets to train and evaluate your AI model. Ensure a representative distribution of scores in both sets.

Model Training:

Use the labeled dataset to train your text evaluation AI model, as discussed in the previous responses. Choose an appropriate model architecture based on the size of your dataset and the complexity of the task.

Iterative Improvement:

As you gather more labeled data, consider periodically retraining your model to improve its performance. This iterative process helps the model learn from additional examples and enhances its ability to evaluate solutions.

Remember that the quality of your labeled dataset is crucial for the success of your AI model. Regularly review the annotation process, address any challenges or questions from annotators, and refine the annotation guide if necessary. Additionally, involve domain experts to ensure that the evaluation criteria align with the goals of assessing circular economy solutions.

rounds.Prompt: do you know if there is anyway we can use an AI to do this?
rounds.Answer:
Yes, you can use AI to assist in the labeling process, although it's important to note that some level of human involvement is usually necessary to ensure the quality and accuracy of the labeled data. Here are a few approaches where AI can be utilized in the labeling process:

Active Learning:

Active learning is a semi-supervised learning technique where the model actively selects the most informative samples for human annotation. The model can start with a small labeled dataset and iteratively request annotations for the most uncertain or ambiguous instances. This reduces the amount of manual effort required while maximizing the learning from each annotation.

Assisted Labeling:

Use AI to suggest labels for human review. An AI model can provide initial predictions for the evaluation criteria, and human annotators can verify, adjust, or correct these suggestions. This accelerates the labeling process while maintaining human oversight.

Clustering and Topic Modeling:

Apply clustering or topic modeling techniques to group similar solutions together. Annotators can then assign scores to entire clusters, reducing the manual effort needed for individual solutions within a cluster. This approach assumes that solutions in the same cluster are likely to have similar scores.

Pre-trained Language Models:

Leverage pre-trained language models like BERT or GPT to extract features and representations from the text data. Although these models are typically used for supervised learning, you can employ them to generate embeddings for your solutions and use clustering or other techniques to group similar solutions.

Rule-based Approaches:

Develop rule-based systems or heuristics to automatically assign scores based on certain patterns or keywords in the text. This can be a quick way to provide initial labels, but it may not capture the full complexity of the evaluation criteria.

While these approaches can speed up the labeling process, it's crucial to validate the AI-generated labels through human review. Human annotators play a key role in ensuring the quality and interpretability of the labeled dataset. Additionally, incorporating feedback from annotators into the model training process can further enhance its performance over time.

Always be cautious about bias and limitations in the AI model's predictions, and regularly assess the model's performance to identify areas where human intervention and refinement are necessary.

def clean_text(text):
    # Convert to lowercase
    text = text.lower()

    # Remove special characters and numbers
    text = ''.join([char for char in text if char.isalpha() or char.isspace()])

    # Tokenize the text
    tokens = word_tokenize(text)

    # Remove stop words
    stop_words = set(stopwords.words('english'))
    tokens = [word for word in tokens if word not in stop_words]

    # Lemmatization
    lemmatizer = WordNetLemmatizer()
    tokens = [lemmatizer.lemmatize(word) for word in tokens]

    # Join the tokens back into a single string
    cleaned_text = ' '.join(tokens)

    return cleaned_text

# Apply the text cleaning function to 'problem' and 'solution' columns

def two_largest_prime_factors(n):
    i = 2
    factors = []
    while i * i <= n:
        while n % i == 0:
            factors.append(i)
            n //= i
        i += 1
    if n > 1:
        factors.append(n)
    
    unique_factors = list(set(factors))
    unique_factors.sort(reverse=True)

    return tuple(unique_factors[:2])

import random

def generate_significantly_different_factors(n):
    factors = []
    for i in range(1, int(n**0.5) + 1):
        if n % i == 0:
            factors.append(i)
            if i != n // i:
                factors.append(n // i)

    factors.sort()

    # Picking a factor from two-thirds the way along the list
    index = len(factors) * 2 // 3
    factor1 = factors[index]

    # Calculating the second factor
    factor2 = n // factor1

rounds.Prompt: How can I create a Mac Automator workflow to show the Safari start page when Command-W is pressed, but only when there is only one open regular tab?

Creating a Mac Automator workflow to show the Safari start page when Command-W is pressed, but only when there is only one open regular tab, involves a combination of Automator and AppleScript. Here's a step-by-step guide on how to set it up:

Open Automator:

Launch Automator from your Applications folder or by searching for it in Spotlight.

Configure the Workflow:

In the Actions Library (left pane), search for "Run AppleScript" and drag it to the workflow area on the right.

Write the AppleScript:

Replace the default AppleScript template in the "Run AppleScript" action with the following script:

[[CODE_1_0]]
This AppleScript checks if there is only one regular tab open in Safari (not including pinned tabs), and if so, it sets the current tab's URL to "about:blank," effectively showing the Safari start page.

Save the Workflow:

Go to "File" and choose "Save..."

Give your service a name, such as "Close Safari Tab to Show Start Page."

Click "Save."

Configure Keyboard Shortcut:

Open "System Preferences" on your Mac.

Navigate to "Keyboard" > "Shortcuts."

Select "Services" from the left sidebar.

Scroll down to the "General" section and find your service (it should be under "Text").

Click on the service name to the right, and then click the "Add Shortcut" button.

Enter the desired keyboard shortcut, such as Command-W.

Ensure that the shortcut doesn't conflict with any existing shortcuts.

Now, when you press Command-W in Safari with only one regular tab open, it will close the tab and show the Safari start page. Please note that this workflow won't work if there are multiple tabs open, including pinned tabs, as it specifically checks for a single regular tab.

on run {input, parameters}
    tell application "Safari"

from pptx import Presentation

def get_shape_type(shape):
    """
    Get the type of a shape.
    """
    if shape.has_text_frame:
        return "Text Box"
    if shape.has_chart:
        return "Chart"
    if shape.has_table:
        return "Table"
    if shape.type == 3:  # Type 3 corresponds to a picture
        return "Picture"
    return "Unknown"

def main(pptx_file):
    # Load the PowerPoint presentation
    presentation = Presentation(pptx_file)

    # Iterate through each slide
    for slide_number, slide in enumerate(presentation.slides, start=1):
        print(f"Slide {slide_number} - Shapes:")
        
        # Iterate through each shape on the slide
        for shape_number, shape in enumerate(slide.shapes, start=1):
            shape_type = get_shape_type(shape)
            print(f"  Shape {shape_number}: {shape_type}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    pptx_file = "your_presentation.pptx"  # Replace with the path to your PowerPoint file

rounds.Answer:
To replace the text in a PowerPoint slide text box using Python, you can use the python-pptx library. Here's a script that demonstrates how to do this:

[[CODE_11_0]]
In this script:

Load the PowerPoint presentation using Presentation.

Access the specified slide and text box using the slides and shapes attributes.

Check if the shape is a text box by verifying the presence of the text attribute.

Replace the text in the text box by assigning the new text to the text attribute.

Save the modified presentation to a new file using presentation.save.

Make sure to replace "your_presentation.pptx" with the path to your PowerPoint presentation file, specify the desired slide number, text box index, and provide the new text you want to insert. The modified presentation will be saved as "modified_presentation.pptx."

from pptx import Presentation

def replace_text_in_text_box(pptx_file, slide_number, text_box_index, new_text):
    # Load the PowerPoint presentation
    presentation = Presentation(pptx_file)

    # Access the specified slide and text box
    slide = presentation.slides[slide_number - 1]  # Slide index is 0-based
    text_box = slide.shapes[text_box_index]

    # Check if the shape is a text box
    if hasattr(text_box, "text"):
        # Replace the text in the text box
        text_box.text = new_text

        # Save the modified presentation to a new file
        modified_pptx_file = "modified_presentation.pptx"
        presentation.save(modified_pptx_file)

        print(f"Text in text box on Slide {slide_number}, Text Box {text_box_index} replaced.")
        print(f"Modified presentation saved to '{modified_pptx_file}'")
    else:
        print("The specified shape is not a text box.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    pptx_file = "your_presentation.pptx"  # Replace with the path to your PowerPoint file
    slide_number = 1  # Change this to the desired slide number
    text_box_index = 0  # Change this to the desired text box index
    new_text = "This is the new text."  # Replace with the text you want to insert

    replace_text_in_text_box(pptx_file, slide_number, text_box_index, new_text)

rounds.Prompt: in SPSS how do you generate frequency results without outputting statistics?
rounds.Answer:
In IBM SPSS Statistics, if you want to generate frequency tables without displaying statistics (such as mean, median, standard deviation, etc.), you can do so by modifying the output options. Here are the steps to achieve this:

Run Your Frequency Analysis:

Start by running your frequency analysis as you normally would:

Go to the "Analyze" menu.

Select "Descriptive Statistics."

Choose "Frequencies."

Select Variables:

In the "Frequencies" dialog box, select the variable(s) for which you want to generate frequency tables.

Open "Statistics" Dialog:

In the "Frequencies" dialog box, click the "Statistics" button.

Unselect All Statistics:

In the "Statistics" dialog box, unselect all the statistical measures you don't want to include in your output. This includes options like mean, median, mode, standard deviation, etc. You can uncheck these options individually.

Click "Continue":

After deselecting the unwanted statistics, click the "Continue" button to return to the "Frequencies" dialog box.

Generate Frequency Tables:

In the "Frequencies" dialog box, you should see that the statistics you deselected are no longer checked. You can now click the "OK" button to generate your frequency tables without the unwanted statistics.

By following these steps, you can produce frequency tables in SPSS without displaying any additional statistics in the output.

How to Write a Newsjacking Blog Post

This just in -- people love reading the news online, and if there’s an opportunity for you to write about a piece of news that can or does directly impact your target audience, you should take it.

Newsjacking refers to the practice of capitalizing on the popularity of a news story to amplify your sales and marketing success. The term was popularized due to David Meerman Scott's book "Newsjacking: How to Inject Your Ideas into a Breaking News Story and Generate Tons of Media Coverage".

There are two different approaches to newsjacking: the immediate rundown of what’s happening and the look back of what happened (alongside what to expect after the initial news break settles). Alternatively, you could publish an initial post to alert readers of the breaking news and then edit once more details arise.

One thing to note with newsjacking: if the topic is or could be perceived as sensitive, be very careful with your writing and positioning. Your decision to cover the story and/or the approach you take in your post could be controversial and negatively impact your brand.

What’s Happening Now/Next [Optional]

If the story is still breaking, you may want to leave this blank. However, if the dust has settled and you have reliable information on what the ripple effects of this news story will be, mention them here so readers know what to expect.

If the story you’re covering impacts a larger audience than your niche readership (say, a new government regulation impacting many industries), narrow down the scope of the implications of this event to your specific reader. Maybe you’re writing for the hardware industry, and new trade regulations will impact shipments and prices of raw materials to manufacturers. In that case, talk about how the new law can or could disrupt or impact that part of a reader’s business.

rounds.Prompt: How can I make a  wide data set in google sheets in a long format
rounds.Answer:
To convert a wide data set in Google Sheets to a long format, you can use the "UNPIVOT" function or utilize a combination of other functions such as QUERY, ARRAYFORMULA, and TRANSPOSE. Here's a step-by-step guide on both methods:

Method 1: Using UNPIVOT function (Available in newer versions of Google Sheets):

Open your Google Sheets document and navigate to a new sheet or a blank area where you want to create your long-format data set.

In the first cell of the new sheet, enter the following formula: =UNPIVOT(SourceSheet!A1:D, "New Header Column", "New Value Column")

Replace SourceSheet!A1:D with the range of your wide data set.

Replace "New Header Column" with the desired header name for the column that will contain the original header values.

Replace "New Value Column" with the desired header name for the column that will contain the corresponding values.

Press Enter to execute the formula. The wide data set will be transformed into a long format in the new sheet.

Method 2: Using QUERY, ARRAYFORMULA, and TRANSPOSE functions:

Open your Google Sheets document and navigate to a new sheet or a blank area where you want to create your long-format data set.

In the first cell of the new sheet, enter the following formula:

=ARRAYFORMULA(QUERY({TRANSPOSE(SourceSheet!A1:A), TRANSPOSE(SourceSheet!B1:D)}, "SELECT * WHERE Col2 IS NOT NULL", 1))

Replace SourceSheet!A1:A with the range of your original headers in the wide data set.

Replace SourceSheet!B1:D with the range of your data values in the wide data set.

Press Enter to execute the formula. The wide data set will be converted into a long format in the new sheet.

In both methods, make sure to replace SourceSheet with the actual name of the sheet containing your wide data set. Adjust the range (A1:D or B1:D) as per your specific data.

Note: The first column in the long format will contain the original header values, and the second column will contain the corresponding values. If you have additional columns in the wide data set, they will be appended as additional columns in the long format.

rounds.Prompt: can one use unpivot on multiple columns?
rounds.Answer:
Yes, the UNPIVOT function in Google Sheets allows you to unpivot multiple columns simultaneously. You can specify multiple columns as part of the source range in the UNPIVOT function. Here's how you can use UNPIVOT on multiple columns:

Open your Google Sheets document and navigate to a new sheet or a blank area where you want to create your long-format data set.

In the first cell of the new sheet, enter the following formula:

=UNPIVOT(SourceSheet!A1:D, "New Header Column", "New Value Column", {"Column1", "Column2", "Column3"})

Replace SourceSheet!A1:D with the range of your wide data set.

Replace "New Header Column" with the desired header name for the column that will contain the original header values.

Replace "New Value Column" with the desired header name for the column that will contain the corresponding values.

Modify {"Column1", "Column2", "Column3"} with the actual names of the columns you want to unpivot. You can add or remove columns as per your requirement.

Press Enter to execute the formula. The specified columns from the wide data set will be transformed into a long format in the new sheet.

Goal: Count the frequency of each individual item in the dataset and keep only those that meet the minimum support threshold (i.e., the minimum number of times an item must appear).

Process:

Scan the entire dataset.

Count how often each item occurs.

Remove items that do not meet the minimum support threshold.

Sort the remaining items in descending order of frequency.

Step 2: Construct the FP-Tree

Input: A frequency table and the dataset.

Goal: Build a compact data structure (FP-Tree) that represents the transactions in a condensed form, preserving the frequency of items.

Process:

Take each transaction from the dataset.

Sort the items in the transaction based on the frequency order from the frequency table.

Insert the sorted items into the FP-Tree:

Start from the root.

For each transaction, follow the path of items already in the tree.

If the path exists, increment the count for that node; otherwise, create a new node for the item.

Step 3: Mine Frequent Itemsets

Create a conditional FP-Tree (a sub-tree) for each item by gathering all the paths that contain that item (i.e., the conditional pattern base).

Use these paths to find the frequent itemsets involving that item.

Repeat this process for each item in the frequency table, working backward from the least frequent to the most frequent.

Step 4: Generate Conditional FP-Tree

Process:

For each item in the conditional pattern base, construct the FP-Tree.

Recursively repeat the process to mine the frequent itemsets from the conditional FP-Tree.

Step 5: Construct the Frequent Patterns

Goal: Combine the mined frequent itemsets to construct the final set of frequent patterns.

Process:

Each frequent itemset found in the recursive FP-Growth steps is combined with the base items.

"""Smart turn analyzer base class using ML models for end-of-turn detection.

This module provides the base implementation for smart turn analyzers that use
machine learning models to determine when a user has finished speaking, going
beyond simple silence-based detection.
"""

import asyncio
import time
from abc import abstractmethod
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from typing import Any, Dict, Optional, Tuple

import numpy as np
from loguru import logger
from pydantic import BaseModel

from pipecat.audio.turn.base_turn_analyzer import BaseTurnAnalyzer, BaseTurnParams, EndOfTurnState
from pipecat.metrics.metrics import MetricsData, SmartTurnMetricsData

# Default timing parameters
STOP_SECS = 3
PRE_SPEECH_MS = 0
MAX_DURATION_SECONDS = 8  # Max allowed segment duration
USE_ONLY_LAST_VAD_SEGMENT = True

class SmartTurnParams(BaseTurnParams):
    """Configuration parameters for smart turn analysis.

    Parameters:
        stop_secs: Maximum silence duration in seconds before ending turn.
        pre_speech_ms: Milliseconds of audio to include before speech starts.
        max_duration_secs: Maximum duration in seconds for audio segments.
    """

    stop_secs: float = STOP_SECS
    pre_speech_ms: float = PRE_SPEECH_MS
    max_duration_secs: float = MAX_DURATION_SECONDS
    # not exposing this for now yet until the model can handle it.
    # use_only_last_vad_segment: bool = USE_ONLY_LAST_VAD_SEGMENT

class SmartTurnTimeoutException(Exception):
    """Exception raised when smart turn analysis times out."""

    pass

class BaseSmartTurn(BaseTurnAnalyzer):
    """Base class for smart turn analyzers using ML models.

    Provides common functionality for smart turn detection including audio
    buffering, speech tracking, and ML model integration. Subclasses must
    implement the specific model prediction logic.
    """

    def __init__(
        self, *, sample_rate: Optional[int] = None, params: Optional[SmartTurnParams] = None
    ):
        """Initialize the smart turn analyzer.

        Args:
            sample_rate: Optional sample rate for audio processing.
            params: Configuration parameters for turn analysis behavior.
        """
        super().__init__(sample_rate=sample_rate)
        self._params = params or SmartTurnParams()
        # Configuration
        self._stop_ms = self._params.stop_secs * 1000  # silence threshold in ms
        # Inference state
        self._audio_buffer = []
        self._speech_triggered = False
        self._silence_ms = 0
        self._speech_start_time = 0
        # Thread executor that will run the model. We only need one thread per
        # analyzer because one analyzer just handles one audio stream.
        self._executor = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=1)

    @property
    def speech_triggered(self) -> bool:
        """Check if speech has been detected and triggered analysis.

        Returns:
            True if speech has been detected and turn analysis is active.
        """
        return self._speech_triggered

    @property
    def params(self) -> SmartTurnParams:
        """Get the current smart turn parameters.

        Returns:
            Current smart turn configuration parameters.
        """
        return self._params

    def append_audio(self, buffer: bytes, is_speech: bool) -> EndOfTurnState:
        """Append audio data for turn analysis.

        Args:
            buffer: Raw audio data bytes to append for analysis.
            is_speech: Whether the audio buffer contains detected speech.

        Returns:
            Current end-of-turn state after processing the audio.
        """
        # Convert raw audio to float32 format and append to the buffer
        audio_int16 = np.frombuffer(buffer, dtype=np.int16)
        audio_float32 = np.frombuffer(audio_int16, dtype=np.int16).astype(np.float32) / 32768.0
        self._audio_buffer.append((time.time(), audio_float32))

        state = EndOfTurnState.INCOMPLETE

        if is_speech:
            # Reset silence tracking on speech
            self._silence_ms = 0
            self._speech_triggered = True
            if self._speech_start_time == 0:
                self._speech_start_time = time.time()
        else:
            if self._speech_triggered:
                chunk_duration_ms = len(audio_int16) / (self._sample_rate / 1000)
                self._silence_ms += chunk_duration_ms
                # If silence exceeds threshold, mark end of turn
                if self._silence_ms >= self._stop_ms:
                    logger.debug(
                        f"End of Turn complete due to stop_secs. Silence in ms: {self._silence_ms}"
                    )
                    state = EndOfTurnState.COMPLETE
                    self._clear(state)
            else:
                # Trim buffer to prevent unbounded growth before speech
                max_buffer_time = (
                    (self._params.pre_speech_ms / 1000)
                    + self._params.stop_secs
                    + self._params.max_duration_secs
                )
                while (
                    self._audio_buffer and self._audio_buffer[0][0] < time.time() - max_buffer_time
                ):
                    self._audio_buffer.pop(0)

        return state

    async def analyze_end_of_turn(self) -> Tuple[EndOfTurnState, Optional[MetricsData]]:
        """Analyze the current audio state to determine if turn has ended.

        Returns:
            Tuple containing the end-of-turn state and optional metrics data
            from the ML model analysis.
        """
        loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
        state, result = await loop.run_in_executor(
            self._executor, self._process_speech_segment, self._audio_buffer
        )
        if state == EndOfTurnState.COMPLETE or USE_ONLY_LAST_VAD_SEGMENT:
            self._clear(state)
        logger.debug(f"End of Turn result: {state}")
        return state, result

    def clear(self):
        """Reset the turn analyzer to its initial state."""
        self._clear(EndOfTurnState.COMPLETE)

    def _clear(self, turn_state: EndOfTurnState):
        """Clear internal state based on turn completion status."""
        # If the state is still incomplete, keep the _speech_triggered as True
        self._speech_triggered = turn_state == EndOfTurnState.INCOMPLETE
        self._audio_buffer = []
        self._speech_start_time = 0
        self._silence_ms = 0

    def _process_speech_segment(self, audio_buffer) -> Tuple[EndOfTurnState, Optional[MetricsData]]:
        """Process accumulated audio segment using ML model."""
        state = EndOfTurnState.INCOMPLETE

        if not audio_buffer:
            return state, None

        # Extract recent audio segment for prediction
        start_time = self._speech_start_time - (self._params.pre_speech_ms / 1000)
        start_index = 0
        for i, (t, _) in enumerate(audio_buffer):
            if t >= start_time:
                start_index = i
                break

        end_index = len(audio_buffer) - 1

        # Extract the audio segment
        segment_audio_chunks = [chunk for _, chunk in audio_buffer[start_index : end_index + 1]]
        segment_audio = np.concatenate(segment_audio_chunks)

        # Limit maximum duration
        max_samples = int(self._params.max_duration_secs * self.sample_rate)
        if len(segment_audio) > max_samples:
            # slices the array to keep the last max_samples samples, discarding the earlier part.
            segment_audio = segment_audio[-max_samples:]

        result_data = None

        if len(segment_audio) > 0:
            start_time = time.perf_counter()
            try:
                result = self._predict_endpoint(segment_audio)
                state = (
                    EndOfTurnState.COMPLETE
                    if result["prediction"] == 1
                    else EndOfTurnState.INCOMPLETE
                )
                end_time = time.perf_counter()

                # Calculate processing time
                e2e_processing_time_ms = (end_time - start_time) * 1000

                # Extract metrics from the nested structure
                metrics = result.get("metrics", {})
                inference_time = metrics.get("inference_time", 0)
                total_time = metrics.get("total_time", 0)

                # Prepare the result data
                result_data = SmartTurnMetricsData(
                    processor="BaseSmartTurn",
                    is_complete=result["prediction"] == 1,
                    probability=result["probability"],
                    inference_time_ms=inference_time * 1000,
                    server_total_time_ms=total_time * 1000,
                    e2e_processing_time_ms=e2e_processing_time_ms,
                )

                logger.trace(
                    f"Prediction: {'Complete' if result_data.is_complete else 'Incomplete'}"
                )
                logger.trace(f"Probability of complete: {result_data.probability:.4f}")
                logger.trace(f"Inference time: {result_data.inference_time_ms:.2f}ms")
                logger.trace(f"Server total time: {result_data.server_total_time_ms:.2f}ms")
                logger.trace(f"E2E processing time: {result_data.e2e_processing_time_ms:.2f}ms")
            except SmartTurnTimeoutException:
                logger.debug(
                    f"End of Turn complete due to stop_secs. Silence in ms: {self._silence_ms}"
                )
                state = EndOfTurnState.COMPLETE

        else:
            logger.trace(f"params: {self._params}, stop_ms: {self._stop_ms}")
            logger.trace("Captured empty audio segment, skipping prediction.")

        return state, result_data

Your binary was built as dynamically linked aarch64

rounds.Answer:
Got it — your snippet is extracting the program interpreter path embedded in BusyBox, which is correct. The reason you’re seeing:

ERROR: Could not find interpreter Requesting program interpreter: /lib/ld-linux-aarch64.so.1

is simply:

✅ BusyBox is dynamically linked, and when you try to run it (or anything that depends on it), the kernel looks for the ARM64 dynamic loader at exactly that path inside your rootfs:

/lib/ld-linux-aarch64.so.1

…but your rootfs doesn’t currently contain that loader file (and probably not the rest of the ARM64 shared libs either).

What you should do next in your script (conceptually)

1) Copy the dynamic loader into your rootfs

You already extracted INTERP from readelf. Now you need to copy it from the toolchain sysroot into the rootfs at the same absolute path.

In other words, if:

INTERP=/lib/ld-linux-aarch64.so.1

SYSROOT=/path/to/aarch64/sysroot

Then the file you must copy from host is:

${SYSROOT}/lib/ld-linux-aarch64.so.1

and it must land in:

${OUTDIR}/rootfs/lib/ld-linux-aarch64.so.1

Also: make sure ${OUTDIR}/rootfs/lib exists.

2) Copy all shared libraries BusyBox needs

The interpreter alone is not enough. BusyBox will also need things like:

libc.so.6

possibly libm.so.6

libresolv.so.2

libdl.so.2

…depending on how it’s built.

You discover these via readelf -d (NEEDED entries) or ldd (but ldd doesn’t work nicely across arch unless you use QEMU).

So your script should:

parse NEEDED libs from BusyBox

locate them inside ${SYSROOT}

copy them into the correct library directory inside rootfs (commonly /lib and/or /lib/aarch64-linux-gnu)

3) Create the expected directory layout

On many Ubuntu/Debian aarch64 sysroots, libs live under:

/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/

/usr/lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/

So your rootfs must mirror that directory structure.

Why you hit this right now

You’re building a minimal rootfs and dropped in BusyBox, but you haven’t yet populated the rootfs with the ARM64 runtime (dynamic loader + glibc libs). So when your build/test step tries to run something inside that rootfs (or you chroot / execute BusyBox), it fails immediately with “missing interpreter”.

Quick checks to run (fast debugging)

Check what BusyBox expects:

[[CODE_7_0]]
Check whether your rootfs has it:

[[CODE_7_1]]
Check BusyBox dependencies:

[[CODE_7_2]]
If the loader file is missing: that’s the immediate cause of the error.

The most common “student mistake” here

Copying libs into the wrong place, like:

putting ld-linux-aarch64.so.1 into /lib64 or /usr/lib

or copying it but not preserving the exact pathname from INTERP

The pathname must match exactly what’s embedded in the binary.

One more important note (so you don’t chase ghosts)

Even after you copy the loader + libs, you still can’t run that ARM64 BusyBox directly on an x86_64 host unless you use QEMU user emulation (or you’re actually running on an ARM64 target). So depending on what you’re doing next:

If you’re doing chroot ${OUTDIR}/rootfs /bin/busybox ... on x86_64 → you’ll also need qemu-aarch64-static inside the rootfs (or use systemd-nspawn with qemu, etc.)

If you’re building an initramfs and booting it in QEMU (full system emu) → you’re fine; loader + libs are what matter.

If you paste:

echo $SYSROOT

output of readelf -l ... | grep interpreter

output of readelf -d ... | grep NEEDED

…I’ll tell you exactly which files/directories you should copy for your specific sysroot layout (Ubuntu toolchain sysroots differ a bit).
